q-346165.worked_solution:
We want to express the area $A$ between the function $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+1$ and the $x$-axis, between $x=0$ and $x=3.$

This can be expressed as the definite integral of $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+1$ between the lower limit $x=0$ and the upper limit $x=3,$ as follows:

$$
A={\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+1\,\text{d}x
$$

q-346173.name: Question 3
q-346173.problem:
Express ${\int }_{1}^{5}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+2)\,\text{d}x$ as the limit of a left Riemann sum.

*Hint: Write down the missing expression in terms of $i$ and $n.$*

${\int }_{1}^{5}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+2)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[(\operatorname{arctan}⁡($
{{field-1}}
$)+2)\cdot \frac{4}{n}]$
q-346173.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{5}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+2)\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+2,$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=5.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{5-1}{n}=\frac{4}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+2)\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{4}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{4i}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\,1+\frac{4i}{n}\,)+2)\,\cdot \frac{4}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-73160.name: Question 4
q-73160.problem: What is ${\int }_{-4}^{-2}-5{x}^{-2}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
q-73160.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{j}=a+jΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{-2}-5{x}^{-2}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=-5{x}^{-2},$ the lower bound is $a=-4,$ and the upper bound is $b=-2.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{-2-(-4)}{n}=\frac{2}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{-2}-5{x}^{-2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[f(-4+j\cdot \frac{2}{n})\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[f(-4+\frac{2j}{n})\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[-5{(-4+\frac{2j}{n})}^{-2}\cdot \frac{2}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

What is ∫−4−2−5x−2dx expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[−5(4jn)−4⋅4n]
b
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[−5(−4+2jn)−2⋅2n]
c
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[−5(4+2jn)−2⋅2n]
d
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[−5(jn)−2⋅1n]
e
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[−5(−2+4jn)−2⋅4n]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑j=0n−1f(xj)⋅Δx,

where Δx=b−an and xj=a+jΔx.

In the definite integral

∫−4−2−5x−2dx,

the function is f(x)=−5x−2, the lower bound is a=−4, and the upper bound is b=−2. So, we have

Δx=−2−(−4)n=2n,

and therefore

∫−4−2−5x−2dx=limn→∞∑j=0n−1f(xj)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑j=0n−1[f(−4+j⋅2n)⋅2n]=limn→∞∑j=0n−1[f(−4+2jn)⋅2n]=limn→∞∑j=0n−1[−5(−4+2jn)−2⋅2n].

q-113884.name: Question 5
q-113884.problem: What is ${\int }_{1}^{5}{e}^{x-1}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
q-113884.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{5}{e}^{x-1}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={e}^{x-1},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=5.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{5-1}{n}=\frac{4}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}{e}^{x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{4}{n})\,\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{4i}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{1+4i/n-1}\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{4i/n}\cdot \frac{4}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-346174.problem:
Express ${\int }_{1}^{10}{x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x$ as the limit of a left Riemann sum.

*Hint: Write down the missing expression in terms of $i$ and $n.$*

${\int }_{1}^{10}{x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[($

q-346174.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{10}{x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={x}^{1/2},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=10.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{10-1}{n}=\frac{9}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{10}{x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{9}{n})\cdot \frac{9}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{9i}{n})\cdot \frac{9}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(\,1+\frac{9i}{n}\,)}^{\,1/2}\,\cdot \frac{9}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Find the function f(x) and the value of b, given that ∫−πbf(x)dx=limn→∞∑k=0n−1[cos2⁡(−π+πkn)⋅πn].

a
f(x)=cos2⁡x and b=0
b
f(x)=cos2⁡x and b=π2
c
f(x)=cos2⁡(x+π) and b=0
d
f(x)=cos2⁡(x−π) and b=π
e

EXPLANATION

A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows: ∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑k=0n−1f(xk)⋅Δx where Δx=b−an and xk=a+kΔx.

Notice that we're given that the lower limit a=−π.

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that Δx=πn. Therefore, πn=b−(−π)n⟹b=0.

Consequently, xk=−π+πkn and f(xk)=cos2⁡xk.

Hence, ∫−π0cos2⁡xdx=limn→∞∑k=0n−1[cos2⁡(−π+πkn)⋅πn].

Therefore, the correct answer is f(x)=cos2⁡x and b=0.

q-113931.name: Question 13
q-113931.problem: What is ${\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
q-113931.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=\pi .$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{\pi -0}{n}=\frac{\pi }{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(0+k\cdot \frac{\pi }{n})\cdot \frac{\pi }{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(\frac{\pi k}{n})\cdot \frac{\pi }{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi k}{n})\cdot \frac{\pi }{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

What is ∫0πsin⁡xdx expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑k=1n[sin⁡(kn)⋅1n]
b
limn→∞∑k=1n[sin⁡(kn)⋅πn]
c
limn→∞∑k=1n[sin⁡(πkn)⋅πn]
d
limn→∞∑k=1n[sin⁡(kπn)⋅1πn]
e
limn→∞∑k=1n[sin⁡(πkn)⋅1n]
Submit

EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as ∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx, where xk=a+kΔx and Δx=b−an.

In the definite integral ∫0πsin⁡xdx, the function is f(x)=sin⁡x, the lower bound is a=0 and the upper bound is b=π. So, we have Δx=π−0n=πn.

Therefore, ∫0πsin⁡xdx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(0+k⋅πn)⋅πn]=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(πkn)⋅πn]=limn→∞∑k=1n[sin⁡(πkn)⋅πn].

q-73180.problem: What is ${\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
q-73180.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=-2{x}^{3},$ the lower bound is $a=-2$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-(-2)}{n}=\frac{5}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(-2+k\cdot \frac{5}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(-2+\frac{5k}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[-2{(-2+\frac{5k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{5}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

What is ∫−23−2x3dx expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(−2+5kn)3⋅5n]
b
limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(2+kn)3⋅1n]
c
limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(5+2kn)⋅2n]
d
limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(5kn)−2⋅5n]
e
limn→∞∑k=1n[−(−1+5kn)3⋅5n]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx,

where xk=a+kΔx and Δx=b−an.

In the definite integral

∫−23−2x3dx,

the function is f(x)=−2x3, the lower bound is a=−2 and the upper bound is b=3. So, we have

Δx=3−(−2)n=5n.

Therefore,

∫−23−2x3dx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(−2+k⋅5n)⋅5n]=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(−2+5kn)⋅5n]=limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(−2+5kn)3⋅5n].

q-113932.name: Question 15
q-113932.problem: What is ${\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
q-113932.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={x}^{5},$ the lower bound is $a=1$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{2-1}{n}=\frac{1}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(1+k\cdot \frac{1}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(1+\frac{k}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[{(1+\frac{k}{n})}^{5}\cdot \frac{1}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-346221.problem:
What is ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

*Hint: Write down the missing expression in terms of $i$ and $n.$*

${\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}$
{{field-1}}
$\cdot \,\frac{\pi }{6n}$
q-346221.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x),$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=\pi /6.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{\pi /6-0}{n}=\frac{\pi }{6n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f(0+i\cdot \frac{\pi }{6n})\cdot \frac{\pi }{6n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f(\frac{\pi i}{6n})\cdot \frac{\pi }{6n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi i}{6n})\cdot \frac{\pi }{6n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi i}{2n})\cdot \frac{\pi }{6n}.\end{aligned}
$$
